source.title: Leave-one-out Distinguishability in Machine Learning
source.authors: Jiayuan Ye; Anastasia Borovykh; Soufiane Hayou; R. Shokri

record.tranche_reason: Extends study of generalization-adjacent memorization and influence to leave-one-out leakage, including activation-function comparisons in NNGPs and SGD-trained networks. It does not measure train/test error gaps directly.
record.gate_note: Tests activation choice as a determinant of per-record leakage, a related property of memorization. Other findings concern LOOD, reconstruction, membership inference, and influence, which do not measure the listed claim versions directly.
record.test_reason: The study measures leave-one-out information leakage, membership-inference performance, influence, and reconstruction. None tests V1–V8. In particular, measuring self-influence does not test V8's effect of removing highly memorized examples on held-out accuracy.
record.authors_conclusion: The record accurately summarizes the authors' intended conclusion: Gaussian-process modeling provides an analytical framework connecting leakage, influence, and memorization, and query optimization enables training-data reconstruction. The authors also conclude that smooth activations yield higher leakage and report this direction for SGD-trained networks. However, the NNGP numerical sentence reverses that direction, so the record should not present the NNGP empirical comparison as internally consistent.
record.recipe_differences: Studies leave-one-out distinguishability and per-record leakage, not test-error generalization under the listed interventions. Includes analytic NNGP experiments and SGD-trained networks.
record.method_sensitivity: Activation choice changes measured leakage; depth increases the stated ReLU–GeLU LOOD gap. Data-dependent normalization can make an optimized query's LOOD slightly exceed that at the differing point. The reported NNGP and NN perturbation scales with maximum leakage differ.

fits_no_version.finding: The authors conclude that GeLU yields greater leakage than ReLU, and report that direction for SGD-trained networks. The NNGP numerical sentence states the opposite direction.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Activation choice affects leave-one-out leakage, with higher leakage under GeLU in the reported neural-network experiment; the NNGP comparison requires resolving an internal reporting inconsistency.

fits_no_version.finding: Optimized multi-query sets yielded lower LOOD than a single query at the differing record in all reported trials.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In the tested NNGP settings, multi-query optimization did not improve leakage over querying the differing record.

fits_no_version.finding: Training-data-dependent normalization allowed optimized queries with slightly higher leakage than the differing record.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Training-data-dependent normalization can move the query of greatest observed leakage away from the differing record.

fits_no_version.finding: Within differing groups, the highest-LOOD record was recovered more frequently than the lowest-LOOD record, with 80% of optimization runs converging.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Single-query LOOD is associated with recovery frequency in the tested group reconstruction experiments.

fits_no_version.finding: Peak leakage along sampled perturbations occurred at zero perturbation for NNGPs and generally near the differing record for trained networks.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Queries at or near the differing training record often maximize observed leave-one-out leakage along tested perturbation directions.

record.problems: The paper studies leave-one-out leakage and influence rather than held-out accuracy or train/test gaps. Some comparisons are stated directionally without numeric values or uncertainty. NNGP is an analytic model and the appendix notes a performance gap from trained neural networks; empirical NN activation comparisons cover 20 randomly chosen differing records.
record.rows_left_out: No claim-version rows apply: the reported measures concern leakage, membership-inference AUC, reconstruction, or influence, not the behaviors named by V1–V8. All directly relevant findings on those topics are recorded under versions ['none'].

untested.parts: Random-label fitting capacity and held-out accuracy under natural versus random labels.
Test error as width increases beyond interpolation.
Held-out error comparisons between convolutional and fully connected networks and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizer generalization under specified tuning budgets.
Batch-size effects on held-out performance under fixed epochs and adapted recipes.
Dropout and weight-decay effects on held-out error.
Magnitude-aware weight sharpness and its correlation with generalization gaps.
Held-out accuracy after removing highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: All row states are cannot_determine relative to V1–V8 because their measures address different constructs. This does not imply that the reported leakage or reconstruction effects are absent. The study cites Feldman and Zhang's memorization definition and estimation approach without testing or relying on V8's accuracy-removal finding.

versions.untested_parts: Does not compare fitting random labels with generalization on natural labels.
No width sweep measuring test error past interpolation.
No convolutional versus fully connected test-error comparison.
No adaptive optimizer comparison on held-out performance.
No batch-size comparison of held-out performance.
Does not measure magnitude-aware sharpness or its association with train/test generalization gaps.
Does not remove memorized examples and measure the resulting test accuracy.

rows.subject: NNGP fully connected neural networks
rows.operation_detail: Measured per-record LOOD under ReLU activation
rows.value: under ReLU is more than 1.1× higher than LOOD under GeLU in 95% cases
rows.locator: Section 6, Experimental results on NNGP; Figure 5
rows.note: Compares leakage, not held-out error or the generalization gap.
rows.check: Leakage does not measure any listed version. The numerical sentence reports ReLU LOOD exceeding GeLU by over 1.1× in 95% of cases, contradicting the surrounding text and Figure 5 caption, which assert higher leakage under GeLU. Preserve and flag this inconsistency; the intended numerical direction cannot be established from the supplied text.

rows.subject: NNGP fully connected neural networks
rows.operation_detail: Compared the depth trend in per-record LOOD for ReLU and GeLU

conditions.value: fixed differing data; ReLU versus GeLU

rows.measure: Gap in LOOD between activation functions as depth changes
rows.value: the gap between LOOD under ReLU and LOOD under GeLU grows with the depth
rows.locator: Section 6, Experimental results on NNGP; Figure 5
rows.note: The reported textual depth trend is for leakage.
rows.check: The reported depth trend concerns leakage, not any listed generalization effect. The direction of the activation comparison is internally inconsistent in Section 6.

rows.subject: fully connected network
rows.stage_stated: deep neural network trained via SGD
rows.operation_detail: Compared per-record leakage measured by membership-inference AUC across activation choices
rows.value: DNNs with GeLU activation incurs higher per-record leakage (MIA performance in AUC score) compared to DNNs with ReLU activation
rows.locator: Section 6, Experimental results on NNs; Figure 5 and caption
rows.note: The text states the comparison direction but gives no numeric AUC values.
rows.check: The directional comparison is accurately reported for 20 differing records, but MIA AUC cannot establish any listed version.

rows.subject: NNGP
rows.operation_detail: Compared KL-divergence LOOD between smooth and non-smooth activation functions

conditions.value: smooth (such as GeLU) versus non-smooth (such as ReLU)

rows.value: smooth activations induce higher LOOD (information leakage) than non-smooth activations
rows.locator: Section 6, conclusion from Propositions 6.1 and G.1
rows.note: The authors state the theoretical implication for NNGPs; this is not a train/test error-gap measurement.
rows.check: This is an authors' theoretical interpretation, not an empirical measurement row. Proposition 6.1 bounds leakage using proximity to a constant kernel; comparing upper bounds alone does not establish an ordering of actual leakage. No listed version is measured.

rows.subject: NNGP fully connected neural networks
rows.operation_detail: Measured optimized multi-query LOOD and compared with LOOD at the single differing data record
rows.baseline: LOOD value from the single differing data record
rows.value: in all evaluation trials, the LOOD values obtained from the optimized m queries are lower than the LOOD value from the single differing data record
rows.locator: Appendix E.1, LOOD under multiple queries
rows.note: This leave-one-out result concerns leakage, not generalization error.
rows.check: The value matches Appendix E.1, but it compares results of query optimization with a single-query baseline. It measures attack optimization performance, not any listed version; it also does not prove that every possible multi-query set leaks less.

rows.subject: NNGP
rows.operation_detail: Compared the optimized query's KL LOOD with the differing point's LOOD under data-dependent training-data normalization

conditions.value: per-channel mean and standard deviation of training dataset

rows.value: The optimized query has a slightly higher LOOD than differing point
rows.note: A stated qualification to the query-at-differing-point result; not a generalization-gap measure.
rows.check: Figure 10 reports slightly higher optimized-query leakage under training-data-dependent normalization. This concerns query location and leakage, not generalization; 'partial' is not a state supported for any listed version.

rows.subject: NNGP
rows.operation_detail: Compared optimized queries with differing-group points in leave-one-group-out experiments

conditions.value: 10 rounds with 10 independent runs per round

rows.measure: Recovery frequency for differing points by optimized queries
rows.value: the differing data point with the highest single-query LOOD was recovered 61% of the times, whereas the one with the lowest single-query LOOD was recovered only 8% of the times
rows.note: Reports reconstruction frequency, not test accuracy.
rows.check: The 61% and 8% recovery frequencies concern reconstruction optimization, not held-out accuracy. The text discusses these observations among converged runs; retain the reported 80% convergence qualification.

rows.subject: NNGP

conditions.value: five randomly chosen for visualization; 70 for statistical pattern
Q = S + x · R, x ∈ [−50, 50], R ∈ L∞ unit ball

rows.value: the scale of perturbation with maximal information leakage is x = 0.000 ± 0.000 for NNGPs
rows.check: The reported peak perturbation scale matches Figure 4, but measures leakage along sampled perturbation directions, not any listed version or unrestricted global maximality.

rows.subject: deep neural networks
rows.size_stated: fully connected network, depth 10 and width 1024 (Figure 5 caption)
rows.operation_detail: Compared MIA performance around perturbations of the differing data

conditions.value: Q = S + x · R, x ∈ [−50, 50], R ∈ L∞ unit ball

rows.measure: Scale of perturbation with maximal MIA performance
rows.note: The authors say MIA is generally highest near differing data; the reported NN peak scale is not exactly zero.
rows.check: The reported peak scale matches Figure 4, but measures MIA performance along sampled perturbation directions. Its nonzero mean does not establish a partial generalization effect. The architecture is attributed from Figure 5 rather than explicitly specified in Figure 4.
